extricate

/EKS-trih-kayt/ - the stress falls on EKS · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Extricate means to disentangle or free from something.

Rosa spent half the reception extricating herself from a conversation that restarted every time she edged toward the door.

Example

The drone came down in a kite-flying park, and the club's youngest member spent an hour on a ladder extricating it, easing the tangled line off one rotor at a time until the machine lifted free.

Extricate is more precise than free or remove because it implies a real entanglement and careful work — the drone was not simply picked up but worked loose from a snarl that resisted.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

free: Free is the plain, all-purpose word for letting something go, and it implies no struggle at all. Extricate earns its extra syllables only when the freeing takes work: something tangled, wedged, or trapped has to be worked loose against real resistance.

disentangle: Disentangle keeps its eyes on the tangle itself — undoing the knots and loops, strand by strand. Extricate looks at the captive instead: you extricate the drone, the driver, or yourself from whatever holds on, with patience and effort.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

entangle: snarl something up in loops and knots

ensnare: trap something deliberately

Where it sits · how hard-won the freedom is

loosen → release → extricate

loosen vs. extricate: Loosen is far milder than extricate — the grip eases a little, but the thing is still caught; to extricate is to work it all the way free.

release vs. extricate: Release is milder than extricate: it simply lets go, while extricating means working something free from a snarl that fights back.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ex-: out

Root — tric: tangles, hindrances (Latin tricae)

Suffix — -ate: verb ending: to make or do

Put it together: Ex- (out) + tric (tangles, hindrances — Latin tricae) + -ate (verb ending) = to get out of the tangles. The Romans used tricae for knots, snarls and petty troubles alike, and the root still means scheming entanglement in intrigue. To extricate something is to bring it out of the snarl — literal string or a contract's fine print.

Use the root in a new word: intrigue: The ambassador's memoir promises a chapter on the intrigue that cost her predecessor his post.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / vivid

Extricate earns its length when the freeing takes work — rescue crews extricate drivers, lawyers extricate clients, and you extricate yourself from an awkward promise. If nothing resisted, plain free or remove is honest. The word keeps its picture of tangles, so it pairs naturally with nets, wreckage, red tape, and long conversations.
